plotting_plan.title: Global Distribution of Freshwater FIB Monitoring
plotting_plan.objective: Global hexbin density map (Robinson projection) of freshwater FIB observation counts with an ecosystem-composition summary, exposing spatial sparsity, the concentration in the US/Europe/Canada, and the apparent void over Russia/China that reflects an open-data sharing gap.

plotting_plan.title: Sampling Objectives and Mismatched Frequencies
plotting_plan.objective: Locator map plus stacked point time series for three Wisconsin sites sampled daily, monthly, and quarterly, contrasting sampling cadence with monitoring objective and showing that gaps in sampling are not trends.

plotting_plan.title: Quantifying the Actionability Gap
plotting_plan.objective: Two-panel figure: a site data-volume survival curve and a bar distribution of per-site sampling return intervals, highlighting that only about 7 percent of multi-sample sites achieve daily or near-daily sampling.

plotting_plan.title: High-Frequency Monitoring Reveals Transient and Chronic Pollution
plotting_plan.objective: Global locator map plus three 2023 high-frequency E. coli line-chart time series (Euclid Beach USA, River Lune UK, Taruheru River NZ) against the 235 CFU per 100 mL safe threshold, showing transient spikes at one site and chronic exceedance at the other two, and demonstrating that low-frequency sampling misrepresents safety in both cases.

plotting_plan.title: Global Safety of High-Frequency Monitoring Sites
plotting_plan.objective: Global scatter map of high-frequency E. coli sites colored by per-site exceedance rate, paired with a donut (pie) chart summarizing the overall split of 77.6 percent safe versus 22.4 percent unsafe across 235 thousand samples.

introduction_strategy.hook_hypothesis: Fecal indicator bacteria, and Escherichia coli in particular, are the primary worldwide tool for judging whether inland fresh waters used for recreation and drinking-water supply are safe from waterborne pathogens.
introduction_strategy.problem_gap_hypothesis: The public, harmonized freshwater FIB monitoring record is failing public health on two measurable axes at once: it is spatially unequal, with most openly shared data concentrated in the United States, Europe, and Canada in a way that reflects an open-data sharing barrier as much as a true collection gap; and it is temporally rigid, dominated by weekly to quarterly sampling that is poorly matched to the rapid, weather-driven dynamics of fecal contamination. All claims are scoped to the freshwater FIB observations actually compiled here (rivers, lakes, and reservoirs) and to the regions and indicators represented in those data; no completeness is claimed for unsampled regions.
search_directions: Find highly cited papers and authoritative reports establishing the global public-health burden of waterborne fecal pathogens and the risk of fecal contamination in recreational and drinking water
Search for review or survey papers on global water-quality monitoring networks, water-quality data availability, and water-related Sustainable Development Goal monitoring
Find foundational papers establishing fecal indicator bacteria such as Escherichia coli and intestinal enterococci as indicators of fecal contamination and human health risk
Find papers on open environmental data, FAIR data principles, and barriers to publishing national water-quality monitoring data in machine-readable form
Find foundational papers establishing the short-term temporal variability of fecal indicator bacteria, including rainfall-driven first-flush spikes and rapid decay within days

related_work_strategy.overview: Investigate four bodies of prior work to position this dataset and its two findings: existing water-quality data compilations, the indicator and threshold basis for FIB monitoring, the temporal-variability and high-frequency monitoring literature, and the environmental open-data and data-sharing literature. Searches are scoped to material published on or before June 2026.

subsections.subsection_title: Global and Harmonized Water-Quality Data Compilations
subsections.methodology_cluster: Multi-source aggregation and harmonization of water-quality observations
subsections.sota_investigation_mission: Identify prior efforts that aggregated and harmonized water-quality or fecal indicator observations across national networks and portals, and determine their geographic, parameter, and temporal coverage. Do not search for works published after June 2026.
subsections.limitation_hypothesis: Existing compilations are typically single-nation or single-region, are not focused on freshwater fecal indicators, or do not characterize the spatial sharing structure and temporal sampling cadence of the record.
limitation_search_queries: global harmonized water quality database fecal indicator bacteria coverage gaps
Water Quality Portal multi-source harmonization limitations
GEMStat global water quality data spatial coverage gaps
subsections.bridge_to_our_method: We assemble a freshwater-focused, ten-source harmonized FIB record and explicitly characterize its spatial sharing gap and its temporal sampling cadence rather than only its contents.

subsections.subsection_title: Fecal Indicator Bacteria, Thresholds, and Health Risk
subsections.methodology_cluster: FIB indicators and regulatory safety thresholds for recreational water
subsections.sota_investigation_mission: Find the regulatory and epidemiological basis for Escherichia coli and enterococci thresholds in fresh and marine recreational waters, including the recommended freshwater single-sample and geometric-mean thresholds, and identify why E. coli is the standard freshwater indicator.
subsections.limitation_hypothesis: Safety thresholds are defined for single-sample or geometric-mean compliance and implicitly assume representative sampling, an assumption that low-frequency, season-limited monitoring violates.
limitation_search_queries: EPA 2012 recreational water quality criteria E. coli beach action value 235
EU bathing water directive E. coli enterococci classification thresholds
fecal indicator bacteria epidemiology gastrointestinal illness risk recreational water
subsections.bridge_to_our_method: We adopt the freshwater E. coli safe threshold to quantify how sampling cadence changes the apparent safety of a water body.

subsections.subsection_title: Temporal Variability and High-Frequency Monitoring of FIB
subsections.methodology_cluster: Short-term FIB dynamics, event-based sampling, and predictive nowcasting
subsections.sota_investigation_mission: Find work characterizing sub-daily to weekly fecal indicator variability, first-flush dynamics, and studies that compare daily versus weekly or monthly sampling or that use rainfall, turbidity, and discharge to predict recreational water safety in near real time.
subsections.limitation_hypothesis: High-frequency and predictive approaches are demonstrated only at a few sites, while most monitoring remains calendar-based and low-frequency, so it both misses transient spikes and can misrepresent chronically polluted waters.
limitation_search_queries: daily versus weekly fecal indicator bacteria sampling recreational water management
first flush stormwater runoff E. coli temporal variability rapid decay
predictive nowcasting model beach water quality rainfall turbidity discharge
subsections.bridge_to_our_method: We quantify at global scale how rare daily sampling is and use high-frequency case studies to show that low-frequency sampling misrepresents both transient and chronic contamination, so higher-frequency data improve management even where pollution is chronic.

subsections.subsection_title: Open Environmental Data and Data-Sharing Barriers
subsections.methodology_cluster: Open data, FAIR principles, and access barriers in environmental monitoring
subsections.sota_investigation_mission: Find literature on open-data policies, FAIR data, and barriers to sharing national environmental and water-quality monitoring data, including comparisons to the international sharing of meteorological data.
subsections.limitation_hypothesis: Substantial national monitoring data exist but are not published in open, machine-readable, harmonized form, producing an apparent data void that is in fact a sharing gap.
limitation_search_queries: FAIR data environmental monitoring water quality open access barriers
national water quality monitoring data not publicly available sharing
international meteorological data sharing model environmental data WMO
subsections.bridge_to_our_method: Our regional shares and explicit source inventory make the distinction between collection gaps and sharing gaps measurable and motivate international data-sharing norms.

content_bullets: State that fecal indicator bacteria are the primary tool for protecting public health in inland fresh waters and that a harmonized global picture has been lacking.
Introduce the compiled freshwater dataset of 5,314,791 observations from ten public sources standardized to CFU per 100 mL.

Report the two central findings: a spatial concentration in the US, Europe, and Canada (89.3 percent of records) reflecting a sharing gap, and a temporal mismatch in which only about 7 percent of multi-sample sites achieve daily or near-daily sampling.
State the implication that rigid low-frequency monitoring misrepresents safety and that open data sharing and higher-frequency or predictive monitoring are needed.
Note key uncertainties: uneven indicator coverage, geographically biased high-frequency sites, and approximations in unit conversion.
Explain in jargon-free terms that bacteria such as E. coli are used worldwide to tell whether rivers and lakes are safe for swimming and drinking.
Describe how the study gathered millions of these measurements from many countries into one comparable dataset.
Explain the two problems found: most shared data come from a few wealthy regions, and most places are tested too infrequently to catch short-lived pollution.
State why this matters for keeping people safe and for fairer global data sharing.

Enumerate the nine point-observation networks and one annual-summary source described in experimental_log.md, with their per-source freshwater contributions and whether each was retrieved by API or manual download.
Note that WQP contributed the majority of records and that GEMStat is a globally sourced compilation spanning many countries.

subsections.subsection_title: The Actionability Gap in Sampling Frequency
content_bullets: Report that of 133,328 sites only 10.8 percent had at least 100 observations and 0.7 percent had at least 500.

Report the return-interval distribution among the 116,489 multi-sample sites: 7.0 percent daily, 9.1 percent weekly, 29.9 percent monthly, 30.7 percent quarterly, 19.2 percent yearly, 4.2 percent longer, and reference the actionability-gap figure.

Report that across 631 high-frequency sites and 235,398 E. coli samples, 77.6 percent of samples were safe and 22.4 percent exceeded the threshold, and that high-frequency sites are almost entirely in North America and Europe.

Present the three 2023 case studies from experimental_log.md: Euclid Beach USA with 18.0 percent exceedance and transient spikes, River Lune UK with 83.7 percent exceedance, and Taruheru River NZ with 62.5 percent exceedance, showing both transient and chronic regimes.

Argue that low-frequency sampling misrepresents safety in both regimes, over-restricting after a single transient spike and under-detecting or misattributing chronic contamination, and reference the case-study and global-safety figures.
